newsitem.title: USA: US Gulf Coast refiners brace for freezing weather.
newsitem.headline: US Gulf Coast refiners brace for freezing weather.

text.p: Crude oil refiners along the U.S. Gulf Coast were bracing Monday for a rare blast of freezing weather expected in the area midweek, officials said.

Refiners dusted off emergency plans to cope with a rare prolonged freeze expected to arrive by Wednesday when an arctic cold front moves through southeast Texas and Louisiana, the nation's key refining region.

"We have a whole series of efforts we go through to weather-proof and freeze-proof our systems," said Ron Embry, a spokesman at Exxon Corp's massive Baytown, Texas refinery, the third largest in the country.

Temperatures were expected to plunge below freezing in the suburbs north of Houston overnight on Tuesday and remain below freezing into Thursday. But warmth from the nearby Gulf waters could push temperatures above freezing in areas south and east of Houston, home to some of the nation's largest refineries.
Crews on Monday began installing insulation on external piping systems and setting up heaters to ensure that piping and critical systems do not freeze in the cold snap.
Hard freezes are a major concern for Gulf Coast refiners, which experienced extensive damage in a prolonged freeze in the late 1980s, meteorologist Jill Hasling said.
"That's when everything froze up and gave the refiners a lot of trouble," she said of a hard freeze that lasted more than 100 hours in southeast Texas.

Freezing temperatures are not unusual in the Gulf Coast area during the winter, but prolonged freezes lasting 10 hours or more are fairly rare. Hard freezes pose the danger of burst pipes cutting off water supplies to refinery cooling systems, and make flares less effective, refinery officials said.
But the cold, dense air also can benefit refinery operations, making jet-fired turbines that power some processing equipment more efficient, the officials said.
